messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Arthur, a 78-year-old divorced database administrator, came to treatment after a prolonged, frightening medical crisis that had begun with what he had first dismissed as “just feeling off.” In the weeks before the hospitalization, he noticed a deepening weakness, a strange shortness of breath, and then a sudden collapse at home that sent him to the emergency department. What followed was, in his telling, a blur of alarms, masked faces, bright lights, and the sharp, antiseptic odor of the hospital room mixed with the metallic smell he later associated with blood and tubing. He was certain at the time that he might die there, and the terror of lying in a bed while his body seemed to fail him left a lasting impression. Since then, ordinary moments at home have not felt ordinary to him. He keeps himself on guard even in his own house, scanning for bodily sensations, listening to every small change in his breathing, and feeling watchful in a way that exhausts him. The hyperalertness is not just vigilance; it is tied to a strong undercurrent of fear, horror, anger, guilt, and shame that flares whenever his attention turns inward.

As the memories of the illness became more settled, they did not become less powerful. When Arthur thinks about those hours in the hospital, he can sometimes smell the same sharp medical odors he noticed then, and that smell pulls the whole scene forward so vividly that he feels as though it is happening again in real time. He described moments when recalling the episode made the room around him seem to recede, while the memory itself felt more real and vivid than his ordinary daily experiences. That vividness has made him distrust the reliability of his own body and his own mind. He has come to believe that his body keeps reacting as if it is still in danger even when he is safe, and that realization has fed a broader conviction that the world is dangerous and unpredictable. Where he once prided himself on being rational and self-contained, he now feels that something fundamental has been broken, and he speaks with sadness about having lost faith in people, in life, and at times in any larger order that might have protected him.

Over the months after discharge, Arthur’s alertness at home became part of daily life. He checks the hallway before bed, pays close attention to the sound of his own pulse, and startles when a sensation he cannot identify passes through his chest. Even in the quiet of his apartment, he remains braced for something to go wrong. That constant watchfulness has made his world feel narrower and more precarious, reinforcing his sense that safety is temporary and fragile. At work, where he still spends part of the week maintaining databases from a small office and occasionally from home, he finds himself interrupted by flashes of bodily fear during long stretches at the screen, and he often needs to stop to make sure he is still okay. He has begun to avoid anything that reminds him too directly of the hospital experience, including certain medical programs on television and conversations about serious illness with friends, because the memories can surge back with such force that he feels engulfed by them. He has told himself that if his body could fail once so suddenly, it could fail again without warning, and that belief has made him increasingly withdrawn and guarded.

Arthur finally sought help when he realized how much of his day was being organized around fear. He was tired of living as though he were still in the hospital bed, tired of being unable to trust his body, and worried that his vigilance was taking over the little life he had built after divorce and retirement from full-time work. What brought him in most urgently was the fear that the next spell of breathlessness or the next vivid smell of antiseptic would send him straight back into that same helpless certainty of dying. He hopes, more than anything, to feel at home in his own body again, though he is also afraid that once he stops scanning for danger, he will be caught off guard and lose whatever small sense of control he has managed to preserve.
